modules.title: History and hypothesis formation
modules.description: Build a structured, person-centred assessment without premature diagnosis.

lessons.title: Start with the person's story
lessons.description: Connect symptoms to function, context and goals.
lessons.text:
Begin with the person's account: onset, mechanism where relevant, symptom behaviour, previous episodes, sleep, work, valued activity and what they hope to regain. Ask open questions before focused questions, and distinguish reported symptoms from observed findings and your interpretation. Pain location alone rarely identifies a single tissue source. Consider comorbidities, medication, communication needs, culture, health literacy and the person's own explanatory model. Agree the purpose of examination, obtain consent and explain how findings will guide the next decision. A useful working hypothesis is provisional: it should explain the available information, identify uncertainty and state what would change your view. The HCPC physiotherapist standards emphasise appropriate assessment, clinical reasoning, informed consent, scope of practice and referral when needed. This course does not authorise independent practice or replace supervised skills training.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. Explain which findings support the working interpretation and which remain uncertain; do not treat a single measure or isolated observation as a diagnosis. Compare options against current guidance for the relevant population, agree a review point, and record the rationale for changes. This material supports independent study only and does not replace individual assessment, supervision, or local protocols.

lessons.title: Risk and differential reasoning
lessons.description: Recognise when the presentation does not fit routine MSK care.
lessons.text:
Do not treat a red-flag checklist as a diagnostic test. Consider the whole presentation, including trauma, systemic illness, cancer history, infection risk, inflammatory features, progressive neurological symptoms and change from the person's usual pattern. The relevance of each feature depends on context, combinations and trajectory. If serious pathology is suspected, stop routine progression and follow local urgent referral pathways. Explain the reason for escalation clearly, document the concern and communicate uncertainty without dismissing symptoms. A normal finding on one test cannot rule out every serious condition. For each fictional case, ask: what alternative explanation must remain in view, what finding would change urgency, and who is the appropriate next professional? Work within competence and seek supervision whenever the findings exceed your role.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. Explain which findings support the working interpretation and which remain uncertain; do not treat a single measure or isolated observation as a diagnosis. Compare options against current guidance for the relevant population, agree a review point, and record the rationale for changes. modules.title: Examination and interpretation
modules.description: Choose tests according to the question, not habit.

lessons.title: Movement, strength and function
lessons.description: Choose measures linked to a decision or patient goal.
lessons.text:
Select examination components because they answer a question. Depending on the presentation and competence, these may include active and passive movement, resisted testing, neurological examination, palpation, balance, gait or a meaningful functional task. Explain each step and obtain ongoing consent. Record position, side, assistance, symptom response and limitations so the result can be interpreted and repeated. A single positive special test or isolated strength score should not be treated as a diagnosis in isolation. Compare the finding with the history, baseline function and other evidence. If a test is unsafe, unlikely to change management or outside scope, do not perform it simply because it is familiar. The aim is a coherent clinical picture rather than the largest possible list of tests.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. Explain which findings support the working interpretation and which remain uncertain; do not treat a single measure or isolated observation as a diagnosis. Compare options against current guidance for the relevant population, agree a review point, and record the rationale for changes. This material supports independent study only and does not replace individual assessment, supervision, or local protocols.

lessons.title: From findings to a working formulation
lessons.description: Separate evidence, interpretation and uncertainty.
lessons.text:
A defensible formulation connects the history, examination and context to a plausible explanation and next step. State what supports the hypothesis, what does not fit, what remains unknown and what would prompt reassessment or referral. Consider symptom irritability, functional impact, patient priorities and relevant medical factors. Avoid equating imaging findings with the source of symptoms or assuming that every asymmetry requires correction. If the presentation changes or the expected trajectory does not occur, revisit the differential rather than repeating the same intervention automatically. Discuss options, likely benefits and burdens, and the person's preferences. Shared decision-making should be documented in language that another clinician can follow.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. Explain which findings support the working interpretation and which remain uncertain; do not treat a single measure or isolated observation as a diagnosis. Compare options against current guidance for the relevant population, agree a review point, and record the rationale for changes. modules.title: Plan, communication and review
modules.description: Translate assessment into a safe, measurable next step.

lessons.title: Goals and shared decisions
lessons.description: Agree meaningful outcomes rather than vague impairment targets.
lessons.text:
Goals are more useful when they describe a task or participation outcome that matters to the person, such as returning to work, climbing stairs or walking to a local shop. Agree how progress will be measured and under what conditions. Discuss reasonable options, uncertainty, the role of self-management and when further assessment is needed. Adapt communication for language, health literacy, disability and distress. A score or impairment measure can contribute, but should not replace the person's experience and priorities. Avoid promising a cure or presenting one treatment technique as universally necessary.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. Explain which findings support the working interpretation and which remain uncertain; do not treat a single measure or isolated observation as a diagnosis. Compare options against current guidance for the relevant population, agree a review point, and record the rationale for changes. lessons.title: Documentation and reassessment
lessons.description: Make clinical reasoning auditable and the follow-up plan clear.
lessons.text:
Document relevant history, examination findings, clinical interpretation, consent, decisions discussed, agreed goals, advice, referral actions and safety-netting. Separate objective observations from the person's report and your clinical impression. State the expected review point and the changes that should trigger earlier contact. Reassessment is not just repeating measurements: it tests whether the original explanation and plan remain plausible. Consider symptoms, function, participation, confidence and adverse responses. Use current local guidance and seek senior or medical input when the pattern is atypical, deteriorating or beyond scope.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. modules.title: Understanding symptoms and goals
modules.description: Relate osteoarthritis to lived function without over-relying on imaging.

lessons.title: Clinical presentation and diagnosis
lessons.description: Use symptom pattern, function and differential reasoning.
lessons.text:
NICE NG226 states that osteoarthritis can usually be diagnosed clinically in people aged 45 or over who have activity-related joint pain and either no morning joint-related stiffness or stiffness lasting no longer than 30 minutes. Routine imaging is not recommended to diagnose typical osteoarthritis unless atypical features suggest an alternative or additional diagnosis. These criteria are guidance, not a substitute for individual assessment or a rule for every age and presentation. Ask about pain, stiffness, swelling, activity, sleep, previous injury, other joints, general health and what tasks have become difficult. An acutely hot swollen knee, fever, major trauma or rapidly worsening inability to bear weight warrants timely medical assessment rather than routine exercise progression.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. lessons.title: Function, expectations and shared decisions
lessons.description: Set meaningful goals and explain what rehabilitation can and cannot promise.
lessons.text:
Osteoarthritis symptoms and radiographic changes do not always correspond closely. Rehabilitation aims to improve function, confidence and quality of life; it cannot promise cartilage repair, complete pain elimination or avoidance of surgery. Ask what matters most: rising from a chair, walking, stairs, work, sleep or recreation. Discuss the likely need for consistent practice and adjustments over time. Weight-related conversations should be respectful and should not be used as a reason to deny support. Explain that some temporary discomfort can occur when beginning exercise, while severe, unusual or persistent worsening requires review. Shared decisions should reflect the person's preferences, health, access and goals.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. modules.title: Exercise selection and progression
modules.description: Choose exercise that matches function, preference and capacity.

lessons.title: Therapeutic exercise as core management
lessons.description: Build a flexible exercise plan around meaningful tasks.
lessons.text:
NICE NG226 recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to the person's needs, including local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness, and says supervised sessions can be considered. There is no single best exercise for everyone. Options may include sit-to-stand practice, knee strengthening, walking, cycling, balance work or water-based activity depending on health, goals, preference and access. Choose exercises that relate to the desired activity and start at a repeatable level. Adjust range, resistance, volume, speed, support and rest based on the person's response. A programme should be feasible enough to repeat, not impressive only during one clinic session.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. Explain which findings support the working interpretation and which remain uncertain; do not treat a single measure or isolated observation as a diagnosis. Compare options against current guidance for the relevant population, agree a review point, and record the rationale for changes. This material supports independent study only and does not replace individual assessment, supervision, or local protocols.

lessons.title: Load, flare-ups and adherence
lessons.description: Adapt dose and recovery rather than using a rigid protocol.
lessons.text:
Agree how the person will monitor response during and after activity. If a flare occurs, temporarily reduce the most demanding component while maintaining safe movement where possible, then build back gradually. Avoid telling people to ignore severe or unfamiliar symptoms. Review delayed soreness, swelling, confidence, sleep and the effect on daily tasks. Behavioural support, reminders, enjoyable activities and a manageable plan can improve adherence. Consider barriers such as transport, cost, caring responsibilities and fear of movement. Exercise dose should be individualised and reviewed rather than prescribed as a universal number of repetitions for all presentations.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. modules.title: Outcomes, referral and long-term management
modules.description: Use reassessment to adapt care and identify when other pathways are needed.

lessons.title: Measure what matters
lessons.description: Pair symptoms with repeatable activity and participation outcomes.
lessons.text:
Select measures that answer the person's question. Examples include a timed chair rise, walking tolerance, stair performance, confidence with a valued task or an appropriate validated questionnaire. Repeat under similar conditions and interpret the result alongside symptoms and participation. A modest change may be meaningful if the person returns to an important activity. If function does not improve, reassess diagnosis, dose, barriers, comorbidity and the person's priorities rather than simply adding more exercises.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. lessons.title: Escalation and onward referral
lessons.description: Recognise atypical presentations and persistent disabling impact.
lessons.text:
Seek medical assessment for atypical symptoms, acute inflammation, significant trauma, new neurological or vascular signs, unexplained systemic symptoms or rapidly deteriorating function. Persistent disabling symptoms despite appropriate non-surgical management may warrant discussion through local pathways, including surgical opinion when suitable. NICE advises that referral decisions should be based on clinical assessment and the impact on quality of life rather than a numerical severity score alone. Do not exclude someone from referral based solely on age, sex, smoking, comorbidity or body size. Explain uncertainty and document the reason for the next step.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. modules.title: Assessment and meaningful goals
modules.description: Connect impairment findings with everyday activity and participation.

lessons.title: The whole impact of stroke
lessons.description: Assess more than strength and movement.
lessons.text:
Stroke may affect movement, sensation, balance, vision, communication, swallowing, cognition, mood, continence, fatigue and participation. NICE NG236 recommends comprehensive assessment that considers previous ability, body-function impairment, activity limitations, participation restrictions, psychological and neuropsychological changes and environmental factors. Ask what the person wants to regain, such as transferring safely, reaching the bathroom, communicating with family or preparing food. Include carers when appropriate while preserving the person's autonomy. Consider communication access, fatigue, cognition, medical stability, home circumstances and consent. A single motor score cannot describe the whole rehabilitation need.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. lessons.title: Functional goal setting
lessons.description: Write goals that are observable, meaningful and revisable.
lessons.text:
Useful goals describe an activity or participation outcome, the conditions in which it matters and how progress will be judged. “Improve strength” may be a treatment target; “stand from the dining chair with the agreed assistance and reach the kitchen safely” is a functional goal. NICE advises that stroke rehabilitation goals should be meaningful, relevant, activity- and participation-focused, challenging but achievable, and include short- and long-term elements. Agree goals with the person and review them when health, fatigue, mood or home circumstances change. Quality, safety, confidence and carer burden may matter as much as speed.

modules.title: Practice, dose and team coordination
modules.description: Plan purposeful repetition in context and adapt to the person's needs.

lessons.title: Task-specific practice and progression
lessons.description: Relate practice to a functional goal and reassess response.
lessons.text:
Practice should be purposeful and connected to the activity the person wants to regain. Depending on presentation, this may include sit-to-stand, reaching, stepping, walking, upper-limb tasks, balance or repeated functional transitions. NICE supports needs-based rehabilitation with content and intensity tailored to goals, medical needs, fatigue, mood and the person's agreement. More repetitions are not automatically better if quality, safety, pain, fatigue or consent deteriorate. Grade assistance, environment, task complexity and rest; document the response and progress when the current level is safe and meaningful. This course cannot teach hands-on handling or replace supervised competency assessment.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. lessons.title: Working with the multidisciplinary team
lessons.description: Coordinate therapy, equipment, communication and transitions.
lessons.text:
A coordinated team may include physiotherapy, occupational therapy, nursing, speech and language therapy, rehabilitation medicine, psychology, dietetics, pharmacy and social care depending on need. The team should share goals and communicate about transfers, equipment, shoulder protection, swallowing, cognition, fatigue, medication, home access and discharge planning. Each professional contributes a different perspective; isolated exercises can miss the practical barriers to participation. Involve family or carers with consent and teach only tasks they can safely support. Review whether the plan remains feasible after discharge and arrange follow-up and equipment through local pathways.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. lessons.title: Red flags and safe mobility
lessons.description: Recognise when routine rehabilitation should pause.
lessons.text:
New neurological deterioration, reduced consciousness, chest pain, severe headache, seizure, aspiration concerns, acute infection or sudden change in function needs prompt medical assessment. Mobility may require modification for blood-pressure instability, cardiac disease, osteoporosis, shoulder pain, neglect, visual-field loss, communication barriers or severe fatigue. Transfers, gait aids and equipment must be selected and taught by appropriately trained professionals in the person's real context. Do not infer safety from one successful attempt or a written guide alone. Follow local emergency and escalation procedures.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. lessons.title: Outcome review and transitions
lessons.description: Track function, participation, adverse responses and changing goals.
lessons.text:
Review symptoms, objective performance, assistance needs, participation, confidence, fatigue and adverse events. A plateau should trigger reassessment of goals, dose, medical factors, environment and barriers rather than an automatic conclusion that rehabilitation has no value. Discharge is a transition, not the end of rehabilitation: coordinate equipment, home adaptations, carers' needs, community therapy and follow-up. Record consent, baseline measures, instructions and escalation advice. Explain uncertainty and avoid promising a fixed recovery timeline.

modules.title: Falls risk and comprehensive assessment
modules.description: Consider the person, health, environment and goals.

lessons.title: Falls are multifactorial
lessons.description: Look beyond lower-limb weakness alone.
lessons.text:
Falls can arise from interacting factors such as gait and balance impairment, strength, vision, hearing, footwear, medication, orthostatic symptoms, cognition, environment, acute illness and confidence. Ask about falls, near-falls, dizziness, loss of consciousness, fear and activity avoidance without blame. A fall is not simply evidence of weak legs, and a generic exercise class may miss treatable contributors. Urgent assessment may be needed after serious injury, concerning head impact, loss of consciousness, chest pain, palpitations, new neurological signs or severe illness. Sudden dizziness or fainting needs appropriate medical review. Use local pathways and stay within professional scope.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. lessons.title: Assessment domains and risk
lessons.description: Use comprehensive assessment to identify modifiable contributors.
lessons.text:
NICE NG249 includes cardiovascular assessment and lying-to-standing blood pressure where appropriate, cognition and mood, dizziness, feet and footwear, functional ability, gait, balance, mobility, strength, hearing and vision, long-term conditions, medication, neurological factors, continence, diet and osteoporosis risk. The World Falls Guidelines similarly support comprehensive multifactorial assessment for people at high risk. Functional tasks may include sit-to-stand, turning, stepping, gait speed, reaching and navigating the person's environment. A screening score can support decisions but is not a diagnosis and does not replace clinical reasoning. Ask what the person wants to keep doing and what changes are acceptable.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. Explain which findings support the working interpretation and which remain uncertain; do not treat a single measure or isolated observation as a diagnosis. modules.title: Progressive exercise and environmental support
modules.description: Develop safe, tailored practice that challenges function.

lessons.title: Balance and strength training
lessons.description: Progress functional tasks according to control and risk.
lessons.text:
NICE NG249 recommends fall-prevention exercise for people who need comprehensive assessment and management. Programmes should be delivered by appropriately trained professionals, progressive and tailored to the person's needs, preferences, goals and abilities, and focus on functional components such as balance, coordination, strength and power with regular review. Possible tasks include repeated chair rises, stepping in different directions, turning, reaching and walking challenges, but selection depends on assessment and safety. Progress only when the current task is controlled, using support, supervision and an appropriate environment. Do not copy a population-level exercise recommendation as a prescription for every person.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. Explain which findings support the working interpretation and which remain uncertain; do not treat a single measure or isolated observation as a diagnosis. lessons.title: Environment and multidisciplinary management
lessons.description: Combine exercise with relevant medical and environmental actions.
lessons.text:
Exercise is one part of a broader plan. Depending on findings, coordinate medication review with a prescriber or pharmacist, vision and hearing assessment, foot care, footwear advice, home hazard assessment, nutrition, hydration, continence support and management of orthostatic hypotension. Do not tell a person to stop medication independently. Occupational therapy may support a validated home hazard assessment; other services may address treatable health risks. Discuss aids and adaptations without treating them as failure. Reassess falls, near-falls, confidence, participation and adverse symptoms over time.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. Explain which findings support the working interpretation and which remain uncertain; do not treat a single measure or isolated observation as a diagnosis. lessons.title: Measure meaningful change
lessons.description: Review falls, near-falls, confidence and daily participation.
lessons.text:
Track falls and near-falls, functional performance, confidence, activity participation and adverse symptoms. A person may become stronger yet remain at risk because of dizziness, vision, medication, environment or cognition. If falls continue, the person develops new symptoms or exercise is not tolerated, reassess the contributing factors and coordinate further review rather than simply increasing exercise difficulty. Discuss goals and risk preferences openly; safety planning should not become blanket restriction of valued activity.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. Explain which findings support the working interpretation and which remain uncertain; do not treat a single measure or isolated observation as a diagnosis. Compare options against current guidance for the relevant population, agree a review point, and record the rationale for changes. This material supports independent study only and does not replace individual assessment, supervision, or local protocols.

lessons.title: Safety-netting and referral
lessons.description: Recognise symptoms that are not routine exercise responses.
lessons.text:
Pause exercise and arrange appropriate medical review for new fainting, concerning dizziness, chest pain, palpitations, new neurological symptoms, acute confusion, severe illness, significant injury or a rapid change in mobility. Local urgency depends on presentation and services. Document what occurred, the person's baseline, observed change, immediate action and handover. Explain who to contact and what symptoms should prompt urgent help. The educational material does not provide a patient-specific exercise prescription or replace a comprehensive falls assessment.

In practice, consider this topic alongside the person's goals, baseline function, relevant history, environmental context, and preferences. Explain which findings support the working interpretation and which remain uncertain; do not treat a single measure or isolated observation as a diagnosis. Compare options against current guidance for the relevant population, agree a review point, and record the rationale for changes. This material supports independent study only and does not replace individual assessment, supervision, or local protocols.

modules.reflectiveActivity: For a fictional person with recurrent falls and dizziness on standing, explain why exercise alone is insufficient and how you would coordinate review.

faqs.question: Is this a ready-made falls exercise prescription?
faqs.answer: No. The course teaches general principles; exercise selection and supervision require individual risk assessment.

faqs.question: Does the course award a certificate or CPD hours?
faqs.answer: No. It is open self-study material without accredited CPD credit or certificate.

faqs.question: How should this guide be used?
faqs.answer: Use it for independent reading and reflection alongside current evidence and local guidance. It does not provide individual clinical advice, assessed competence, accreditation, awarded CPD hours, or a completion certificate.
